title: Agentic AI Governance Dimension for the FLI Safety Index

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The 2025 AI Agent Index from MIT (arXiv:2602.17753) already documents governance and safety features of 30 deployed agentic AI systems across six categories including safety/evaluation, autonomy/control, and ecosystem interaction. It found that only 15/30 agents have published safety frameworks, 25/30 disclose no internal safety results, and 23/30 have no third-party testing. Additionally, the FLI AI Safety Index Summer 2025 already evaluates companies on 33 indicators across six domains. The specific contribution of designing 6-8 agentic governance indicators and scoring companies is largely subsumed by these two existing indices. The remaining gap is a formal integration of agentic-specific indicators into the FLI methodology, but the empirical groundwork is done.

title: Safety Index Sensitivity Analysis: How Robust Are Company Rankings to Indicator Weighting?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Sensitivity analysis of composite indicators via Monte Carlo weight sampling is a well-established methodology (OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators, COINr R package). It has been applied to governance indices like the Resource Governance Index and Good Country Index. However, no published work applies this specific robustness analysis to the FLI AI Safety Index rankings. The FLI index uses 33 indicators with equal weighting across six domains, and the question of whether company rankings (especially the close C+/C cluster) are robust to weight perturbation is unanswered. The methodology is standard but the application to AI safety governance rankings is novel and timely.

title: Incident Reporting Rate Dimension for the AI Safety Index

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The OECD AI Incidents Monitor (AIM) and AIAAIC Repository both catalog AI incidents, and the OECD published a common reporting framework in February 2025. The FLI AI Safety Index Summer 2025 evaluates companies on governance including transparency and incident disclosure. However, no existing work has constructed per-company incident reporting rates from these databases and formally integrated them as a scoring dimension in a safety index. The OECD framework focuses on standardizing reporting, not on scoring companies by their incident rates. The attribution challenge (linking incidents to specific companies) is acknowledged in the literature but not systematically solved. The idea adds value by bridging incident databases with company-level governance scoring, though the data sparseness and attribution problems are real limitations.

title: Evaluating the MIRI TGT Governance Agenda's Technical Assumptions

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: MIRI TGT published its governance research agenda in May 2025, centered on international compute restrictions and an 'Off Switch' for frontier AI. The agenda makes explicit technical assumptions: training compute correlates with capabilities, FLOP thresholds can be set conservatively (10^24 FLOP cap), and compute can be monitored internationally. TGT's own paper 'Declare and Justify' argues evaluations should explicitly state assumptions. However, no external work has systematically evaluated the empirical validity of TGT's core assumptions (compute-capability correlation under algorithmic progress restrictions, semiconductor supply chain monitorability, enforcement feasibility). Apart Research ran a Technical AI Governance Challenge hackathon in early 2026 but no published output systematically tests these specific assumptions.

title: Framing Shift Consequences: Did UK AISI's Rebrand Change Its Research Output?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The UK AI Safety Institute was renamed to the AI Security Institute on February 14, 2025. This rebrand has been widely discussed qualitatively: Opinio Juris (November 2025) analyzed the policy shift, the UK Parliament debated it (CDP-2025-0238), and the Wikipedia article documents the change. AISI published its 2025 Year in Review and a Frontier AI Trends Report. However, no published work has performed a systematic before/after content analysis of AISI's research publications to quantify whether the rebrand changed research topics. The qualitative assessment is that the shift was politically motivated and aligned with US priorities, but empirical measurement of output changes (keyword distributions, topic classification) has not been done. The clear cutoff date and publicly available publication list make this a well-scoped natural experiment.

University AI governance discussions focus primarily on teaching policies (generative AI use in coursework) rather than research lab safety practices. The AAUP published guidance on AI and academic professions but focuses on employment and teaching, not research safety governance. title: India's 2025 AI Governance Guidelines vs. EU AI Act: A Technical Obligations Comparison
